prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, explaining which firms export and invest abroad and how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 alone, credited to Helpman and Melitz. The discussion did not change the configuration, but it did change how I would defend it. The discovery is one idea. Productivity differences across firms drive selection into exporting and foreign investment, so trade reallocates activity within industries and adds a channel for the gains from trade. Melitz (2003) is the originator of the core selection model. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) add the exports-versus-FDI sorting result, and Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition foundations make him a natural co-recipient. The predictions were tested repeatedly in firm-level data for more than twenty years, and where the baseline failed in detail the literature extended the model and kept the selection logic. That is the maturity I look for. I also weigh that it changed the object of analysis in trade and is now used in macro, development and productivity work. The chair's summary shows all eleven files at the same configuration. That convergence comes from one model and shared reasoning patterns, and I give it no weight as merit. I therefore tested the strongest objections instead. The Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum issue is a real attribution limit, but I judge it acknowledgeable in the scientific background and in narrow citation wording. It does not make a two-name award indefensible. The citation I propose names selection and reallocation, and it makes no claim about the size of the welfare gains or about the whole firm-level and quantitative trade literature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter-premia facts that motivated the theory, and Eaton and Kortum developed a parallel Ricardian line. None of them can be credited on this ballot entry, so a Helpman-Melitz award necessarily leaves out important contributors. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is excluded as well. If the Committee defines the achievement as the whole firm-level and quantitative trade programme, the entry is too narrow, and I cannot resolve that from the shortlist, because the quantitative-trade lineage (B037) and a Helpman-Grossman framing (B047) are not on it. The baseline Melitz model's sharper predictions are rejected in detail, and its welfare magnitudes depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions. Part of the new-trade-theory lineage was recognised with Krugman in 2008, so the incremental step could be judged smaller. I think firm selection is conceptually distinct from scale economies with representative firms, but that is a judgement. Finally, B001 is theory-led. Its link to policy practice is more indirect than B006's direct use in merger review and antitrust.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first in his opening to B001 first in round 1. He keeps B006 as the main fallback and says the discovery boundary and credit story of B001 are tighter. He also notes that B001 and B006 together would need five people, more than the three-laureate limit.
responses.response: I agree on the limit. A two-part prize of B001 plus a trimmed B006 would fragment the BLP credit, because Pakes alone would not represent the demand-estimation core. I also see no clean way to put Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes alongside Helpman and Melitz within three people. So I treat B006 as a true alternative to B001 and not as a second part. I note that you and I co-authored a menu-cost paper, and I do not want my agreement to be deference to the chair. My reason for agreeing is the one you give. The B001 boundary is tighter, and the B006 question of whether it is one discovery or two is still open. The alternative that would change my view is a Committee decision to credit demand estimation alone, with a clean Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes citation, and to weigh transferable tools equally with conceptual change. I would then regard B006 as fully competitive.

responses.point: Enflo says she is less comfortable treating the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as only a caveat. In her view, whether the prize covers the model that organised the facts or the facts plus the theory is a judgment about what counts as the discovery, and the record does not settle it.
responses.response: I think this is the right way to state the issue, and it is the question I raised in round 1 as the point where I would move toward B006. After the exchange I land on the narrower reading. The Committee recognises the model that organised the exporter-premia facts and generated the selection and reallocation channel. The facts motivated the theory and tested it, but they did not supply the sorting mechanism or the export-versus-FDI result. Hjalmarsson is also right that Eaton-Kortum is a Ricardian framework distinct from Melitz selection. I accept that this is a judgement about the boundary and not a finding of fact. For that reason I would want the citation to say 'introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory' and to leave the empirical facts and the quantitative lineage to the scientific background. If a majority wanted the empirical facts and the theory credited together, this ballot entry would be the wrong vehicle, and I would say so.

responses.point: Boppart prefers the clean two-name award to adding a third name only to fill the cap, because adding Redding would not close the gap left by the omitted Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
responses.response: I agree. A third name chosen to fill the cap would not repair the attribution problem and would move the citation toward the quantitative strand. In round 1 I asked whether Redding should be credited alongside or instead of the pair. After the exchange I answer no, as long as the discovery is the selection framework. Redding's claim would rise only if the Committee chose to define the achievement as quantitative trade, and that is a different framing from B001, one I cannot assess from this shortlist. I also share your point on Krugman. I would handle it through wording, naming selection across heterogeneous firms so that the citation cannot be read as a repeat of the 2008 scale-economies recognition. Your remark about the welfare sensitivity matters here too, and it is why I would not mention welfare magnitudes in the citation.

responses.point: Strömberg moved B006 down because the demand-estimation and dynamic-model strands, and the roles of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, make the discovery boundary hard to draw. He disagrees that structural IO methods are only methodological, because they revealed facts about market power and welfare that reduced-form work could not.
responses.response: I accept both halves of that. On the boundary, I agree that the Bresnahan question shows how hard it is to cut B006 to three names, and it is one reason I rank B006 second and not first. On methods versus discovery, I agree that your point is substantive and that I should not dismiss B006 as a toolkit. Structural IO has produced evidence on markups, merger effects and welfare that would not otherwise exist. My remaining difference is narrow. B001 changed what the field takes to be the object of analysis and added a theoretical channel for gains, while B006 mainly changed what can be estimated. I agree with the weakness you noted in your own case, that I can state this distinction but cannot show it is a scientific ordering. Because I work on pricing under imperfect competition, I am close to both fields, so I rest the comparison on the discovery-boundary point and on B001's tested predictions, not on my sense of which field matters more.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as acknowledgeable in the background or as a reason the two-name award is too narrow. I now lean to the former, but it is a judgement about what counts as the discovery and not an established fact.

Whether the discovery should be framed as the selection and reallocation framework (B001) or as a broader firm-level and quantitative trade programme. B037 and B047 are not on the shortlist, so I cannot assess how that would change the credited names, and I do not want to assume that Redding or Grossman would then be better placed.
How far the sensitivity of the welfare-gain magnitudes to distributional assumptions should limit the citation. I propose that it not mention magnitudes at all.

Whether B006 can be bounded to a defensible demand-estimation core, and whether the Committee weighs a widely used methodological toolkit equal to a conceptual reorientation. This is the one question on which I would move.

Because the files share one model and similar reasoning, agreement across them is weaker evidence than it looks. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or award history, and my assessment rests on the supplied openings, the chair summary and general knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman, Melitz or any other credited name on the shortlisted entries is apparent from my profile. For transparency, I co-authored a menu-cost paper (IJIO 2026, not on the shortlist) with the chair John Hassler and with Tore Ellingsen. I have disclosed this and I do not treat the chair's move to B001 as a reason for my own position. My research in exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and imperfect-competition pricing is adjacent to trade and industrial organisation, which may bias my reading of B001 and B006. My spouse is Magdalena Andersson, a public fact noted only for disclosure, and no bearing on any shortlisted candidate is apparent. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
